title: A 12-Year-Old Coder Built a Robot to Save His Endangered Language
summary: Imagine a toy that speaks your grandmother’s language — a language so rare that only a few thousand people on Earth still use it. That’s exactly what Danielle Boyer, 25, created with the SkoBot, a customizable robot designed to revitalize Anishinaabemowin, the ancestral tongue of the Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi peoples. The idea struck her in a toy store. “Whenever you’d press [Tickle Me Elmo’s] belly, he would talk and teach you things,” she recalled. “There are toys that teach us in English, but there aren’t toys that teach us Anishinaabemowin.” The stakes are high. In the U.S., fewer than 10,000 people speak the language; in Canada, around 25,000. Some dialects have only a handful of fluent elders. U.S. Indian boarding schools historically punished children for speaking their native languages, accelerating the loss. Today, even when offered in schools, many Native youth see language class as “another homework assignment,” Boyer said. Her solution: make it playful. The SkoBot is a small, shoulder-mounted device that resembles a woodland creature decorated with Native floral designs. It uses a simple form of artificial intelligence — not generative AI, but a trigger-word system that plays pre-recorded audio files. Ask “What is bear?” and it responds, “Bear is makwa, makwa.” Through her nonprofit, Boyer has mentored hundreds of Native kids to build their own bots. One is 12-year-old Holden Hoy from Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. He programmed his SkoBot, named Sabe (Bigfoot), to introduce itself with a joke: “I will not gain sentience and take over the world. Or will I?” At his school’s STEAM Museum, visitors lined up to interact with Sabe. “I’m happy that people are actually coming to this booth,” Hoy said. “I’m really happy that I’m part of the Ojibwe.” For Boyer, whose grandmother is among the last fluent speakers of their dialect, the project is deeply personal. “It is devastating to feel like your language could be lost,” she said. “You lose your culture, you lose a way to describe who you are.”
why_it_matters: Language shapes identity and thought. When a language vanishes, the world loses a unique perspective. This story shows how young people can use technology to preserve their heritage and connect generations, making it a powerful example of innovation and tradition working together.

background_read: The SkoBot is part of a growing worldwide movement to preserve endangered languages. UNESCO estimates that one language dies every two weeks, often with the passing of its last elder speakers.

In North America, many indigenous languages face extinction because of decades of forced assimilation. U.S. Indian boarding schools, which operated into the late 20th century, were designed to erase Native cultures by punishing children for speaking their mother tongues.

Danielle Boyer, a 25-year-old robotics inventor from Michigan, founded a nonprofit called The STEAM Connection to create accessible educational technology. Her project focuses on Anishinaabemowin (the ancestral language of the Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi peoples, also known as the Three Fires Confederacy).
The idea of using low-cost, wearable robots to teach language is a creative blend of technology and cultural preservation, and it has already inspired similar projects in other Native communities.

perspectives.description: The SkoBot brings Anishinaabemowin into children's daily lives through play, helping to reverse the shame once associated with speaking indigenous languages. For Native youth like Holden Hoy, it fosters pride and a sense of belonging, while also creating intergenerational bonds as elders' voices are recorded.

Critics worry that a robot cannot replace the full cultural immersion that fluent human speakers provide, and that relying on devices may not address the deeper trauma caused by forced assimilation. There is also a risk that this approach is seen as a novelty rather than a sustained solution.

Language loss is not unique to North America; it is a global crisis tied to colonization and globalization. The SkoBot fits into a broader trend of digital tools being used for language documentation and revitalization, raising questions about what it truly means to 'save' a language — and who gets to decide.

If the project can scale, low-cost bots could be adapted for hundreds of endangered languages worldwide. The key will be ensuring that communities, not outside corporations, control the recordings and design, so that cultural knowledge stays in the hands of the people it belongs to.
